name: @visuelconcept/wui-gis
description: GIS pages (/gis + /gis/:siteid) — map-based monitoring on MapLibre GL over OpenStreetMap (BSD-3 / ODbL, no licence cost): geo-located assets bound to datapoints with live value overlays on the marker, alarm highlighting taken from the datapoint's own _alert_hdl.._act_state_color so the map agrees with the alarm list, areas (districts / sectors / catchments) as drawn polygons grouping the assets, and a configurable drill-down from map to area to asset to its process or 3D view (/fleet-3d/:atelier, /ampere/:networkid, /mosaic/:board, or the Alarms page scoped to the asset's datapoint). An asset can belong to SEVERAL areas (Asset.areaIds, a multiple-choice list in the inspector; on placement it joins every area whose outline covers the point): each of them lists and counts it, while areaIds[0] is its PRIMARY area — the only one whose badge may absorb the marker when areas collapse, since a marker is drawn once and both the draw-once and no-asset-lost-or-duplicated invariants depend on a single owner. A legacy single areaId is folded into the list on read, and the sanitiser accepts either shape. One click also FITS an area outline around the assets it lists (gis/enclose.ts): a CONCAVE outline, computed in a local metric plane, following the shape the equipment makes instead of a convex hull closed by a long chord across empty ground — which is how the first version read on a real network, as if it had joined the last asset back to the first. The hull is dug inwards chi-shape style, longest boundary edge first, through the nearest asset not yet on the boundary, as long as that keeps the polygon simple; the detour is BOUNDED rather than required to shrink, because the textbook two-shorter-edges rule cannot carve a square bay (reaching an arm’s inner corner always costs one edge longer than the chord across the mouth) and it is the pool, not the geometry, that makes it terminate. The dig threshold is measured in asset SPACINGS so one default fits a city district and a 15 km main, in a narrow band that was measured rather than guessed (1.2–3, default 1.74): a clear C has a mouth only two spacings wide, so a looser factor never digs at all — which is exactly what the first calibration did. The margin is PROPORTIONAL (8 % of the group’s diagonal, floored at 50 m and capped at 500 m) rather than a fixed 150 m that is most of a pumping station and a rounding error on a sector. The ring is the rounded OFFSET of that polygon — sides pushed out along their normals, convex corners arced, reflex corners mitred and cut past four margins — so no marker sits on the boundary, one asset gives a disc and a straight run of valves a capsule instead of a zero-area sliver with nothing to fill. Three guarantees are enforced rather than hoped for: every listed asset ends up inside; the ring never crosses itself (crossing insertions refused, the offset validated and retried at half margin, then the always-offsettable convex outline); and the ring is at most 64 points because that is what the sanitiser keeps and a truncated ring is a DIFFERENT shape — corners capped at 20, ones the margin would hide dropped first, and a hull still oversized after that (a round blob of a hundred assets) enclosed by a disc. Beyond zones the site also holds a NETWORK and information LAYERS, three concepts kept distinct on purpose: an area is GEOGRAPHY (a polygon containing assets, used for grouping and roll-ups), a CONNECTION is TOPOLOGY (a supervised link between two assets — a metro segment, a feeder, a main, a road), a ROUTE is just a NAME for a set of connections (« Ligne 1 ») and a LAYER is CLASSIFICATION (a free tag such as critical or phase-2, with no shape and no containment rule). A connection carries everything an asset carries except a position — a primary datapoint whose _alert_hdl colour PAINTS THE LINE, live readings shown on hover, a drill-down route, zone membership, layer tags, notes — because a feeder has a current and a track section has a status; without that the network would have to be drawn twice, once as geometry and once as invisible assets on top. It is deliberately NOT the same type as an asset: Asset is a point and cluster.ts grids assets in Web-Mercator world pixels, enclose.ts hulls their coordinates, assets are HTML markers while polylines must be GL layers, so paths in Site.assets would have branched every one of those and turned the no-asset-lost invariant into a statement with exceptions. Its ends are REFERENCES (from/to name assets), not coordinates, so dragging a substation drags every line attached to it with nothing recomputed — storing endpoint coordinates desynchronises the network on the first edit, which is how the feature ends up switched off; via only shapes the line between those ends. A connection whose end no longer resolves is DROPPED and counted (an invisible line is worse than none), deleting an asset cascades to its connections, and a self-connection goes the same way. A metro line is NOT one object: the tempting Route{stops[]} with segments implied between consecutive stops breaks the first time a station is inserted, because every later segment shifts by one and so does every datapoint binding attached by index — a silent mis-binding. Segments are therefore explicit objects with stable ids (also physically right: a fault occurs BETWEEN two stations), and a route does not list its stops at all — the order is DERIVED by walking the from/to chain, and a branching line (one plant feeding three reservoirs) returns null rather than an invented sequence. The line tool draws a whole line in one continuous gesture: click assets one after another, each click closing a segment and opening the next, clicks on the map between two assets adding shaping points, and the route picker creating the line on the spot (New line…) so nobody has to fill a form before they can draw. Rendering is three GL layers — an invisible fat hit line (a 3.5 px track is unclickable otherwise), a dark casing that keeps a coloured route legible over a raster basemap, then the dashed-by-kind line — below the area outlines, above nothing, needing no glyphs. Connections are never clustered: lines do not collide like discs, so they stay drawn at every zoom and a faulted feeder is visible even when its zone has collapsed to a badge. Layers are tags with a BROWSER: create, rename, recolour, delete, per-layer visibility, isolate-one, plus a usage count; a tag can also be created straight from an asset by typing a name into its editable Layers field, because the need for a tag is discovered while looking at the asset, not before. Layer VISIBILITY IS NOT STORED — which layers an operator is looking at is a property of the operator, so it is session state (and therefore usable without the edit grant); an untagged object is never hidden and a tagged one survives while at least one of its tags is on. Selecting an asset shows chips for its zones, layers and lines at the top of its panel, and each chip NAVIGATES — a zone chip goes to the zone, a line chip opens its segment. Selecting an area fills the side panel with one card per asset showing that asset live values, alarm-edged when it is in alarm and clickable to open the asset. Stored as GIS_Site DPs, one per site; the overview doubles as the multi-site view with a live in-alarm count per site. Basemap is per site: public OSM tiles, an own XYZ raster server, an own MapLibre vector style, or none at all for an air-gapped plant (assets and areas still draw). Zoomed out the markers group as a three-rung hierarchy — assets, then one badge per area (ringed in the area colour, so it says which zone is in trouble), then one badge for the whole site — on by default and toggled off to draw everything. A badge is a FAULT SYNTHESIS and nothing else: it draws only the number of its assets in alarm, and a group with no alarm is NOT DRAWN AT ALL — zoomed out the map is zones plus trouble, the area polygons saying where the equipment is and a bubble appearing only where something is wrong, so a quiet plant is a quiet map and anything visible on it is something to go and look at. A bubble with nothing to synthesise was still an object the eye had to check and discard, which is the opposite of what a synthesis is for; the member count stays in the badge tooltip. The drop happens in the VIEW rather than by removing quiet groups from the grouping, so "no asset lost or duplicated" stays a testable statement about cluster.ts — with the known consequence that quiet assets folded into a flat-grid cell are absent until you zoom in, there being no polygon to stand in for a grid cell the way there is for an area. An alarmed asset is therefore grouped like any other rather than escaping every badge — it is not hidden, the badge turns alarm-coloured and states how many it swallowed, and one click zooms to exactly those assets, whereas keeping alarms out turned a plant in trouble seen from far out into the very pile of loose discs grouping exists to prevent. The collapse threshold is configurable per area and per site, defaulting to automatic: an area collapses when its extent no longer fits its assets, and the site threshold is DERIVED from the area ones (1.5 zoom levels below the last expanded area, bounded by area-badge overlap) because independent pixel thresholds put both collapses inside one integer zoom step and the area rung would never be seen. An area is always grouped WHOLE or not at all — never a few loose markers plus an anonymous badge holding the rest of the same area: the collapse is measured on the area assets rather than on its ring, on a raw (unpadded) extent, and in automatic mode an area also collapses whenever the flat grid would merge any two of its assets. The grid is anchored in Web Mercator world pixels so panning never re-buckets anything; clicking a badge zooms into exactly its members. In-place edit mode places and drags markers, draws and RESHAPES area outlines (corner handles to drag or click-to-remove, hollow midpoint handles to click-to-insert, a triangle being the protected floor; the drag is buffered in the map component and handed to the page on dragend) and binds datapoints. Asset name plates are drawn only for a disc that is visually on its own (nearest-neighbour distance in world pixels), so a busy map never turns into overlapping text. An AREA is never labelled on the map: its name appears in a tooltip following the cursor while the pointer is over its outline, naming every zone under the cursor since zones may overlap — a dozen permanent plates competing with the asset plates for the same pixels is unreadable, and the polygon and its colour already say where a zone is. Embeds a proposal-only AI assistant (toolless, via the optional /api/ai bridge, hidden unless the deploy enables it and the user holds the edit role) that drafts a whole site — areas and assets, with suggested readings but never a datapoint binding — for review on the map before saving; every proposal is coerced through a sanitiser that drops unusable positions, unknown kinds, dangling area references and off-site links, and caps a runaway answer (64 areas and 10 000 assets per site) — a ceiling against a runaway answer rather than a capacity claim, since three real limits sit below it and did not move when it was raised: one dpConnect per datapoint element (deliberately isolated, so ~30 000 subscriptions at that size), one HTML marker per drawn asset, and the whole site JSON in one WinCC OA String element. Falls back to two demo sites (water network, smart-city district) when the project has no GIS_Site datapoint. Import/export in two formats: native JSON ({kind:gis-sites,version,sites}, all sites or one) round-tripping bindings, readings, drill-down routes, basemap and grouping thresholds; and GeoJSON per site (areas as Polygon, assets as Point, connections as LineString carrying their from/to so the topology is rebuilt rather than frozen, routes and layers as collection metadata since they have no geometry) for QGIS/ArcGIS interop — which is also how surveyed coordinates come back in, correcting the assistant's approximate ones. A native import creates sites, a GeoJSON import fills the open site through the same review-then-Done path the assistant uses, and a FOREIGN layer with no gisType property is read by geometry (polygon=area, point=asset). Every import passes through the same sanitiser as an AI proposal. Frontend only for the page itself — no backend route; maplibre-gl (pinned to 5.x in tools/external-dependencies.mjs) is auto-detected from the vendored page and bundled into it. Ships one OPTIONAL manager, gisSim, a NETWORK simulator for demos and commissioning: it reads the GIS_Site datapoints, gives every asset and every connection a FAMILY from its kind CROSSED WITH THE KIND OF ITS LINKS (a station wired with power connections is a power plant, the same station wired with pipes is a pumping station — the links are the only evidence the model carries), creates one FLAT datapoint per simulated value (GisSim_<assetId>_<element>, GisLink_<connectionId>_<element>) plus the _alert_hdl config on the ones it creates (a binary alert on `defaut`, which is what colours a marker, since the page widens asset.dp to its datapoint — flat rather than a struct per asset for exactly that reason), and then solves the FLOWS over the site topology rather than wobbling each value independently: consumers ask, the sources the graph connects them to supply in proportion to their capacity, each segment carries the sum of what transits it, so taking a plant out moves its cities onto the plants that remain and tripping a segment reroutes the flow or leaves the consumer visibly short. It NEVER writes to a site (bindings are the page's business): its naming rule is the contract, and the companion CLI bind-site.js writes exactly those names into an exported site — same catalogue, so the two cannot drift. Real figures come from `sim:` directives in an object's notes (sim:capacite=5460, sim:demande=15000, sim:etat=0 for a plant shut down for good, sim:famille= to override the resolution); anything unstated is sized from a stable hash of the id, capped at what the topology can actually bring to that consumer. examples/gis-france-nucleaire.json is a ready-to-import site (19 EDF plants, 8 consumption poles, 19 lines) already bound to it. A SECOND topological coupling covers the networks where nothing is consumed and the allocation therefore has nothing to allocate: a segment belongs to a ROUTE, so closing one metro tunnel section thins the service on every other section of that line, raises the delays along it and on the stations at its ends, and leaves the other line on the same map untouched — a property of which segments the author put on which route, needing no configuration. That is also why metro and rail are separate families: a metro section is supervised on its tunnel temperature and its third-rail voltage, a mainline one is not. Ridership and road traffic follow their own daily curve rather than the electrical one, which never falls below ~65 % of its peak and made a station at 4 a.m. read as a rush hour. Beyond the reserved directives, any sim:<element>= key sets THAT element's baseline (sim:affluence=2600 on an interchange), the family's span scaling with it so the relative variability stays the family's; a key naming neither is reported rather than ignored. examples/gis-dubai-metro.json (13 underground stations, 13 sections, 2 lines) is the ready-to-import site for the route coupling.
